frames.narration: A nightly import feeds 10,000 keys, in sorted order, into an ordered map. Two implementations get the same input: a plain binary search tree and an AVL tree, which rotates to stay balanced.

The plain tree never moves a node. Each key is bigger than all before it, so it becomes the right child of the last one. The tree is 10,000 levels deep, building it costs 49,995,000 comparisons, and a lookup averages 5,000.50. It is a linked list with extra pointers.

The AVL tree checks the heights on the way back up after each insert. When one side of a node is 2 levels taller than the other, it rotates: the tall child becomes the parent, and the key order stays the same. Result: height 14, 123,617 comparisons to build, 12.36 per lookup.

The price is 9,986 rotations, about one per insert. Each is a few pointer changes and no key comparison, so it is cheap next to the 49,995,000 comparisons it saves. Red-black trees rotate less (at most 2 per insert) and tolerate a taller tree; AVL keeps the tightest height.

Random order would have spared the plain tree: height 34 and 17.90 comparisons per lookup, against height 16 and 12.56 for the AVL tree. That is why the bug passes tests with shuffled data and collapses on a real import.

Break it: a zigzag order (smallest, largest, next smallest, ...) looks shuffled to a human. The plain tree is again 10,000 levels deep and costs 49,995,000 comparisons. The AVL tree stays at height 17, with 146,639 comparisons and 16,221 rotations.

On disk the unit of cost is a page read, and a billion keys in a balanced binary tree are 30 levels: 30 reads. A B-tree with 100 children per node needs 5 levels, with 500 children 4. It keeps every leaf at the same depth by splitting and merging wide nodes, not by rotating.

In practice: use the ordered map your language ships, which is a balanced tree (often red-black), or a B-tree-based index in a database. Write a plain BST only to learn, and never on data whose order you do not control.
